Executive Summary
- Context: ActiveTech is launching a Smart Fitness Watch in the consumer electronics market targeting health-conscious millennials (ages ~27–43). The category is competitive and fast-evolving, with incumbents (Apple, Samsung, Garmin, Fitbit/Google) and niche players (WHOOP, Oura) shaping expectations around accuracy, battery life, design, and wellness insights.
- Objective: Build a differentiated, profitable go-to-market (GTM) and product strategy that converts health-conscious intent into daily engagement, drives sustainable unit economics, and establishes ActiveTech as a credible wellness tech brand.
- Core Strategy: Position ActiveTech as the “habit-forming fitness watch” that pairs accurate metrics with simple, motivating daily actions. Differentiate on battery life, actionable coaching, and affordability. Leverage a hybrid monetization model (device sale + optional low-friction subscription) and a digitally led, community-centric GTM.

Key Questions
1) What specific value proposition will differentiate ActiveTech with millennials who may already own trackers or smartphones?  
2) Which sub-segments offer the fastest path to traction and advocacy?  
3) What feature set balances user value with cost and time-to-market?  
4) What pricing and monetization model maximizes LTV while maintaining competitive CAC?  
5) Which channels and partnerships are most efficient for acquisition?  
6) Which KPIs will track product-market fit and unit economics?

Market and Competitive Overview
- Trends:  
  - Wearables penetration rising; wellness use cases (sleep, mental health, recovery) growing.  
  - Users demand actionable guidance vs. raw data; privacy and sustainability matter.  
  - Economic sensitivity favors strong value propositions in the $149–$299 range.  
- Competitors:  
  - Apple/Samsung: ecosystem lock-in, strong features, higher ASP.  
  - Garmin: endurance athletes, GPS, long battery life.  
  - Fitbit/Google: wellness at mid-price, broad distribution.  
  - WHOOP/Oura: recovery/sleep, subscription-led.
- Opportunity: A mid-price device with excellent battery life, credible accuracy, and simple, habit-forming coaching that doesn’t require high monthly fees.

Target Audience Segmentation (Health-Conscious Millennials)
1) Fitness Enthusiasts (performance-minded)  
   - Needs: GPS accuracy, HR/HRV, VO2 Max estimate, training load, Strava integration.  
   - Hooks: Battery life, training insights, community challenges.  
2) Lifestyle Improvers (wellness + accountability)  
   - Needs: Sleep tracking, stress score, step/active minutes, reminders, simple coaching.  
   - Hooks: Habit streaks, micro-goals, rewards, affordability.  
3) Biohackers/Quantifiers  
   - Needs: HRV, readiness score, data export/API, rich analytics.  
   - Hooks: Advanced metrics, experiments, integrations.  
4) Budget-Conscious Switchers  
   - Needs: Reliable basics, durability, ease-of-use, value.  
   - Hooks: Price, battery life, privacy.

Positioning and Value Proposition
- Positioning Statement: “ActiveTech helps you turn healthy intentions into daily wins—combining accurate tracking, long battery life, and simple coaching that fits real life.”
- Differentiation Pillars:  
  - Actionable: Daily micro-coaching and habit streaks that drive behavior change.  
  - Enduring: 7–10 day battery life and durable design.  
  - Accurate and Open: Credible sensors with integrations (Apple Health/Google Fit/Strava) and optional data export.  
  - Responsible: Privacy-first controls and sustainable materials/packaging.

Product Strategy (V1 Feature Set)
- Hardware Essentials:  
  - Battery: 7–10 days typical.  
  - Sensors: Optical HR, SpO2 (passive overnight), accelerometer/gyroscope, GPS/GLONASS.  
  - Water resistance: 5 ATM.  
  - Display: Always-on option with power save.  
- Software Essentials:  
  - Core Metrics: Steps, HR, HRV-derived recovery/readiness, sleep staging, stress proxy.  
  - Coaching: Daily readiness score with personalized activity/sleep recommendations, habit streaks, guided goals.  
  - Fitness Modes: Running/cycling/yoga/HIIT with distance/pace/HR zones.  
  - Integrations: Apple Health, Google Fit, Strava; notifications; basic music controls.  
  - Privacy: Clear data permissions, offline mode, on-device processing where feasible.  
- Roadmap (6–12 months):  
  - v1.1: Menstrual cycle tracking, mindfulness sessions, adaptive training plans, more workouts.  
  - v1.2: Open API for advanced users, recovery score refinement, group challenges, employer/insurer integrations.  
  - Hardware v2: Optional ECG, improved GNSS, skin temp.

Monetization and Pricing
- Device Pricing:  
  - Base model: $199–$229 MSRP to undercut premium incumbents while supporting quality.  
  - Premium model (metal build/GNSS upgrade): $279–$299.  
- Subscription (optional, not required for core features):  
  - ActiveTech+ at $5.99–$7.99/month or $59/year.  
  - Value: Advanced insights (readiness trends), guided plans, coach-curated content, advanced analytics, data export/API.  
  - Target attach rate: 20–30% by month 6; minimize core feature lock-in to avoid churn.
- Bundles:  
  - Launch bundle: Device + 3 months ActiveTech+ + premium band.  
  - Partner bundles with gyms, health apps, and employers.

SWOT Analysis
- Strengths: Mid-price value, battery life focus, habit-forming coaching, privacy-forward stance.  
- Weaknesses: New brand credibility, limited ecosystem lock-in, potential sensor parity with incumbents.  
- Opportunities: Wellness coaching gap at mid-price, employer/insurer channels, sustainability differentiation, community-led growth.  
- Threats: Aggressive price cuts by incumbents, iOS/Android platform shifts, supply chain volatility, regulatory scrutiny on health claims.

Porter’s Five Forces (Summary)
- Rivalry: High—established brands and rapid feature diffusion.  
- Buyer Power: Moderate—switching costs are low without ecosystem tie-in.  
- Supplier Power: Moderate—chipsets and sensors relatively concentrated.  
- Threat of Substitutes: High—phones, rings, gym equipment, apps.  
- Threat of New Entrants: Moderate—hardware is capital-intensive; brand trust barrier.

Go-To-Market Strategy
- Positioning Narrative: “Daily wins for real life.” Emphasize habit streaks, readiness-based coaching, long battery, privacy. Demonstrate outcomes (e.g., +X active days/month).
- Channel Mix:  
  - DTC e-commerce (primary) with robust landing pages and financing (Klarna/Affirm).  
  - Marketplaces: Amazon for reach; maintain MAP to protect pricing.  
  - Retail pilots: Best Buy specialty sections, boutique fitness retailers.  
  - Partnerships:  
    - Fitness apps (Strava, Calm/Headspace), boutique gyms (Orangetheory, F45), nutrition apps.  
    - Employers/insurers for subsidized programs; wellness challenges.
- Demand Gen:  
  - Influencers: Micro-creators on TikTok/Instagram/YouTube in fitness/wellness; authentic 30–90 day “habit change” series.  
  - Community: Referral program (give $20, get $20), monthly challenges with leaderboards.  
  - Content: “Daily Wins” blog/newsletter, habit science explainer, success stories.  
  - PR: Wellness + tech outlets; sustainability and privacy angles.  
  - Performance Marketing: TikTok, Instagram Reels, YouTube; creatives centered on habit formation and battery life proof points.
- Offers:  
  - Launch pre-order at $179–$199 with 3 months ActiveTech+.  
  - Trade-in program for old trackers to address e-waste and price sensitivity.

Customer Journey and Funnel
- Awareness: Influencer content, short-form videos, PR.  
- Consideration: Comparison pages vs. Apple/Fitbit/Garmin, social proof, battery and coaching demos.  
- Conversion: Risk reduction—30-day return, 1-year warranty, quick setup videos, online chat.  
- Onboarding: 7-day coaching program to build a streak; push minimal notifications; celebrate early wins.  
- Retention: Weekly progress emails, evolving goals, seasonal challenges, community groups.  
- Expansion: Prompt for ActiveTech+ after 2–3 weeks when baseline established; cross-sell bands/chargers.

KPIs and Dashboard
- Acquisition: CAC by channel, site conversion rate, email waitlist signups, paid media ROAS, influencer CAC.  
- E-commerce: Add-to-cart rate, checkout conversion, ASP, bundle attach rate.  
- Product: Activation rate (device paired within 24h), day-7 and day-30 retention, DAU/MAU, weekly workouts per user, streak adherence, notification opt-outs, feature adoption.  
- Monetization: Subscription attach %, trial-to-paid conversion, monthly churn, ARPU, LTV/CAC ratio.  
- Support/Quality: Return rate, defect rate, NPS/CSAT, battery performance tickets.  
- Operations: COGS, gross margin, inventory turns, stockout days.
- Visualization:  
  - Funnel chart (site visit → purchase → activation → day-30 retention).  
  - Cohort analysis for retention and subscription conversion.  
  - Unit economics dashboard (CAC, ARPU, LTV, margin).  
  - Heat maps for feature usage and drop-offs during onboarding.

High-Level Unit Economics (Assumptions to validate)
- Device COGS target: $90–$120 for base model; aim for 45–55% gross margin at $199–$229 MSRP.  
- Marketing CAC: $60–$100 blended early; target LTV/CAC ≥ 2.5 within 6 months.  
- Subscription: $7/month, 25% attach, 3% monthly churn → payback on CAC improved by 3–6 months.  
- Returns/defects: Keep <6% combined to protect margin.  
- Sensitivity: Battery life or accuracy issues drive returns and NPS down—prioritize QA and clear expectations.

Risk Assessment and Mitigations
- Data privacy/regulatory (GDPR/CCPA): Implement granular consent, data minimization, easy export/delete, HIPAA-avoiding language for non-medical claims.  
- Accuracy claims and expectation management: Publish validation methods, avoid medical claims; provide explainers for metrics.  
- Supply chain disruptions: Dual-source critical components; buffer inventory for launch; forecast scenarios.  
- Platform dependency (iOS/Android updates): Maintain compatibility testing program and rapid OTA updates.  
- Competitive pricing pressure: Differentiate on coaching and community; maintain cost discipline; flexible promotions without brand erosion.

Launch Plan (90-Day and 12-Month)
- 0–30 Days (Pre-Launch)  
  - Finalize MVP feature set and validation tests for battery/accuracy.  
  - Build waitlist and ambassador beta (500–1000 users across segments).  
  - Creative development: habit-change narratives, UGC toolkits, comparison pages.  
  - Lock pricing/MAP, DTC stack (Shopify), fulfillment, returns.  
- 31–60 Days (Soft Launch)  
  - Ship to beta; collect telemetry on battery, HR accuracy, onboarding.  
  - Iterate coaching prompts, tune notification cadence.  
  - Seed 100+ creators with 30-day challenge kits; referral program live.  
  - PR briefings; retail/partner outreach for pilots.  
- 61–90 Days (Public Launch)  
  - Paid campaigns go live; landing pages with clear UVPs and social proof.  
  - Offers: launch bundle + limited-time price.  
  - Support readiness: live chat, knowledge base, fast RMA.  
  - Dashboard in place for daily KPIs; war room cadence to adjust CAC/creative.  
- 12-Month Objectives  
  - Sell 50k–100k units (dependent on budget); reach 25% subscription attach; NPS > 45; day-30 retention > 45%.  
  - Launch v1.1 features; secure 1–2 employer/insurer pilots; open API beta; sustainability report.

Partnerships to Pursue
- Fitness and Wellness: Strava, MyFitnessPal, Calm/Headspace.  
- Employers/Insurers: Virgin Pulse, UnitedHealthcare Motion, regional employers targeting wellness incentives.  
- Retail: Best Buy, REI (for enthusiast segment), Amazon.  
- Sustainability: E-waste recyclers; trade-in partners to reinforce brand values.

Assumptions and Validation Plan
- Millennials value habit coaching and battery life enough to consider switching: Validate via pre-launch surveys and A/B creative testing.  
- Mid-price point is elastic with right value narrative: Test $199 vs $229 vs $249 in pre-orders.  
- Optional subscription increases LTV without blocking core value: Test conversion and churn with 30/60-day trial cohorts.  
- Coaching cadence/UX drives retention: Run experiments on notification frequency and goal-setting.

Next Steps
1) Conduct rapid concept testing with 300–500 target users to prioritize features/messages.  
2) Lock BOM and negotiate with suppliers to hit COGS targets; establish QA gates for sensors and battery.  
3) Build onboarding flow that sets a 7-day habit streak; instrument analytics for step-by-step drop-offs.  
4) Recruit 100 micro-influencers for pre-launch 30-day “Daily Wins” series; define creator compensation tied to CAC.  
5) Finalize DTC stack, customer support SLAs, and return policies; train support team on common issues.  
6) Prepare executive KPI dashboard; set weekly decision cadence for GTM optimization.

This plan provides a clear, differentiated approach to launch and scale ActiveTech’s Smart Fitness Watch with health-conscious millennials, balancing compelling product value, disciplined unit economics, and practical execution.

Practical guide: choosing the right array in C++
- Fixed-size at compile time: use std::array<T, N>. Fast, stack-allocated (if not too large), safe API.
- Variable-size known at runtime with frequent indexing: use std::vector<T>. Contiguous memory, amortized O(1) push_back, O(1) random access.
- C-style T a[N] or new[]: avoid unless interfacing with legacy/low-level code. Easy to make mistakes (bounds, lifetime).
- Large 2D arrays:
  - std::vector<std::vector<T>>: flexible, but rows non-contiguous.
  - Single vector as 2D: std::vector<T> grid(R*C); access grid[r*C + c]; contiguous and cache-friendly.

Complexity quick reference
- Indexing: O(1) for std::array, std::vector.
- Insert/erase at end of vector: amortized O(1). Insert/erase in middle: O(n).
- Resize vector: O(n) to move elements; reserve(n) to pre-allocate capacity.

Common patterns (concise examples)
- Read N and array:
  - vector<int> a(n); for (int i=0;i<n;i++) cin >> a[i];
  - Optimize I/O: ios::sync_with_stdio(false); cin.tie(nullptr);
- Pre-allocate for performance:
  - vector<int> a; a.reserve(n);
- Prefix sums (int to long long to avoid overflow):
  - vector<long long> pref(n+1,0); for (int i=0;i<n;i++) pref[i+1]=pref[i]+a[i];
  - Range sum [l,r] inclusive: pref[r+1]-pref[l]
- Sliding window (sum over size k):
  - long long s=0; for (int i=0;i<k;i++) s+=a[i]; for (int i=k;i<n;i++){ s+=a[i]-a[i-k]; /* use s */ }
- Frequency counting:
  - vector<int> cnt(M,0); for(int x:a){ if(0<=x && x<M) cnt[x]++; }
- Search and sort:
  - sort(a.begin(), a.end());

- Passing arrays to functions:
  - void f(const vector<int>& v) { /* read-only */ }
  - void g(vector<int>& v) { /* modify */ }

- int vector of size 1e6 ≈ 4 MB (plus overhead). 1e7 ≈ 40 MB; check limits.

Executive summary
Objective: Leverage Random Forest on customer transaction data in the banking sector to drive measurable improvements in fraud loss prevention, customer retention, cross-sell effectiveness, and credit risk management. Start with 2–3 high-ROI use cases, establish robust data/model governance, and deploy within a 12-week phased plan.

Business context and key questions
- Context: Banks have rich transactional signals that can predict risk and behavior. Random Forest is a strong, fast-to-deploy baseline for tabular data and can offer explainability via feature importance and SHAP.
- Objectives:
  1) Reduce fraud losses and false positives at alerting.
  2) Improve customer retention by early churn detection.
  3) Increase product penetration through next-best-offer propensity.
  4) Enhance early warning for credit risk deterioration.
- Key questions:
  - Which use cases deliver fastest payback given current systems and data?
  - How will we measure business impact (not just model accuracy)?
  - What latency, explainability, and governance constraints must be met?
  - How do we ensure data privacy, fairness, and model stability over time?

Prioritized use cases (recommend piloting top 2 first)
1) Real-time fraud detection and alert prioritization
- Goal: Maximize prevented fraud while reducing false positives.
- Features: Transaction velocity (per channel/merchant), geo-location distance, merchant category history, time-of-day patterns, device/channel fingerprints, customer RFM (recency, frequency, monetary), deviation from personal baseline.
- Modeling: Class-imbalance handling (class weights, undersampling/SMOTE), time-based splits, threshold optimization for precision/recall trade-offs.
- KPIs: Fraud loss prevented, precision/recall (PR AUC), false positive rate, alerts per 1,000 transactions, average handle time.
- Integration: Sub-200 ms scoring target for card auth; batch for ACH/wire post-monitoring.
- Impact drivers: Fewer false positives improve CX and ops cost; higher recall reduces net losses.

2) Churn prediction (retail banking or cards)
- Goal: Predict likelihood of churn in next 60–90 days to trigger retention actions.
- Features: Declines in transaction frequency/spend, paycheck deposit changes, fee incidence, service interactions, channel usage, competitive payment tokens, life-event markers (e.g., new recurring payments elsewhere).
- KPIs: AUC, lift at top deciles, retention rate uplift, net retained revenue, offer cost per save.
- Activation: Target top-risk deciles with tailored outreach and retention offers.

3) Cross-sell and next-best-offer (propensity)
- Goal: Increase conversion for loans, cards, or savings by targeting high-propensity customers.
- Features: Merchant category spend vectors, recurring payments (e.g., rent vs. mortgage), travel patterns, card-on-file indicators, balance trends, lifecycle signals.
- KPIs: Conversion rate uplift, incremental revenue per contact, contact-to-sale ratio, opt-out/complaint rate.
- Approach: Champion-challenger models and uplift modeling as next step.

4) Credit risk early warning
- Goal: Detect deteriorating repayment capacity before delinquency.
- Features: Declines in income proxies (deposit inflow), rising utilization, cash flow volatility, increased minimum payments, overdraft frequency, new BNPL/credit obligations inferred from transactions.
- KPIs: KS/AUC, bad rate by decile, days of early warning, reduction in NPLs/charge-offs, collections effectiveness.

Data and feature engineering
- Data scope: 12–24 months of transactions; enrich with customer demographics, products, channel logs, devices, merchant data; ensure consent and lawful basis.
- Feature types:
  - Aggregations: RFM, rolling windows (7/30/90 days), ratios (current vs. baseline).
  - Behavioral: Merchant category distributions, seasonality, time-of-day, weekday/weekend.
  - Network/sequence proxies: Counterparty diversity, new merchants, burstiness.
  - Risk/fraud signals: Geodistance vs. home, failed attempts, device changes, MCC mismatches.
- Labeling:
  - Fraud: Confirmed chargebacks or investigator-confirmed cases.
  - Churn: No account activity or closure within a defined window.
  - Cross-sell: Offer acceptance within campaign period.
  - Credit risk: 30+/60+ DPD within horizon.
- Validation:
  - Time-based train/validation/test to avoid leakage.
  - Address imbalance; evaluate with PR AUC for rare-event tasks.
  - Calibrate probabilities (Platt/Isotonic) for business thresholds.

Modeling considerations for Random Forest
- Strengths: Handles nonlinearity, mixed features, robust to noise, fast baseline, intrinsic feature importance.
- Weaknesses: Less interpretable than single trees; may be heavier than gradient boosting for very tight latency; not sequence-native.
- Practical guidance:
  - Benchmark RF against Gradient Boosting (XGBoost/LightGBM) and Logistic Regression; select per use case.
  - Use SHAP for local and global explanations to support compliance and frontline use.
  - Optimize for operating points tied to business KPIs (e.g., loss prevented per alert).

KPI framework and measurement plan
- Fraud: Prevented loss = (fraud value captured at chosen threshold) – (operational cost of alerts + customer friction cost proxy). Track precision, recall, PR AUC, FPR, AHT, and net fraud rate.
- Churn: Retained revenue = incremental saves × average annual contribution margin – retention offer costs. Track AUC, lift, save rate in top deciles, offer ROI.
- Cross-sell: Incremental conversion uplift vs. control; revenue per 1,000 contacts; CPA and LTV-to-CAC.
- Credit risk: Early-warning lead time; reduction in roll rates and charge-offs; collections hit rate uplift.

- Benefits:
  - Fraud: (Baseline fraud losses – post-model losses) – (adj. for displacement).
  - Churn: Incremental retained margin – incentives.
  - Cross-sell: Incremental gross margin from conversions – marketing costs.
  - Credit risk: Reduction in expected loss = PD × LGD × EAD improvements.
- Costs:
  - Data engineering, compute, model dev, integration, tooling, monitoring, staff training, governance reviews.

Ingredients (base)
- Quinoa: 1 cup (rinsed well under cold water to remove bitterness)
- Liquid: 1 to 1.25 cups water or broth (1 cup for firmer grains, 1.25 cups for softer)
- Salt: 1/4 to 1/2 tsp (to taste)
- Optional: 1 tsp oil or butter (reduces foaming, adds flavor)

Yield
- About 3 cups cooked quinoa (serves 3–4 as a side)

Pressure Cooker Settings
- Electric pressure cooker (e.g., Instant Pot):
  - Pressure: High
  - Cook time: 1 minute
  - Release: Natural release for 10 minutes, then quick release any remaining pressure
- Stovetop pressure cooker:
  - Bring to high pressure over medium heat, cook 1 minute, then remove from heat and allow pressure to drop naturally for 10 minutes before opening

Step-by-step
1) Rinse quinoa thoroughly in a fine mesh sieve until water runs clear; drain well.
2) Optional: Toast quinoa on Sauté (or over medium heat) with 1 tsp oil for 2–3 minutes until lightly nutty.
3) Add liquid and salt; stir once to distribute evenly.
4) Seal the cooker.
   - Electric: High pressure, 1 minute. Natural release 10 minutes, then quick release.
   - Stovetop: High pressure, 1 minute. Remove from heat, natural release 10 minutes.
5) Open lid, fluff gently with a fork. Rest 2–3 minutes uncovered to let steam escape for a drier texture.

Adjustments and options
- Texture:
  - Firmer: 1 cup liquid per 1 cup quinoa, same timing.
  - Softer: 1.25–1.5 cups liquid or 2 minutes at pressure.
- Altitude: Above ~3,000 ft, add 1–2 minutes to pressure time or increase liquid by 2–4 tbsp.
- Flavor boosters:
  - Cook in low-sodium vegetable or chicken broth.
  - Add aromatics before sealing: 1 small minced shallot or 1 clove garlic sautéed, 1 bay leaf, or a 2-inch strip of lemon zest.
  - Mix-ins after cooking: chopped herbs, lemon juice, olive oil, toasted nuts, roasted vegetables, feta.
- Meal preps:
  - Cool on a sheet pan to stop carryover cooking; refrigerate up to 5 days or freeze up to 2 months.

Troubleshooting
- Too wet or mushy: Use less liquid next time (reduce by 2–3 tbsp per cup) or vent sooner; spread cooked quinoa to steam off moisture and fluff.
- Too firm or undercooked: Add 2–3 tbsp hot water, reseal, and pressure cook for 0–1 minute; or steam on Warm for 5–10 minutes.
- Bitter taste: Rinse longer, consider a brief toast with oil before adding liquid.

- Herbed lemon quinoa: Stir in 2 tbsp lemon juice, zest, 2 tbsp chopped parsley, 1 tbsp olive oil after cooking.
- Mexican-style: Cook in 50/50 water and salsa, add 1/2 tsp cumin; finish with cilantro and lime.

- Simple ratio chart: quinoa-to-liquid for firm vs. soft.

- Mobility considerations and luggage needs

- Day 1: Arrival and unwind. Check in near Gion/Higashiyama or Kyoto Station. Stroll along Kamo River; explore Teramachi/Kawaramachi. Light dinner at Veg Out or Ain Soph. Journey Kyoto.
- Day 2: Southern Higashiyama. Kiyomizu-dera, Sannenzaka/Ninenzaka, Kodaiji. Tea ceremony in Gion. Dinner: Mumokuteki Cafe & Foods.
- Day 3: Philosophers Path. Nanzen-ji, Eikan-do, walk to Ginkaku-ji; stop at a tea house. Optional evening walk through Yasaka Shrine to Maruyama Park.
- Day 4: Fushimi Inari early morning; Tofuku-ji gardens. Afternoon Uji day trip: Byodo-in, tea tasting. Dinner back in Kyoto.
- Day 5: Arashiyama. Tenryu-ji and bamboo grove, Okochi Sanso Villa; optional Monkey Park. Temple lunch: Shigetsu (shojin ryori, reserve). Sagano Scenic Railway if interested.

- Day 7: Northwest temples. Kinkaku-ji, Ryoan-ji, Ninna-ji. Lunch/dinner at Ajiro (shojin ryori near Myoshin-ji, reserve). Explore Myoshin-ji temple complex.
- Day 8: Kurama to Kibune hike. Soak at Kurama Onsen (if desired). Seasonal riverside dining in Kibune (confirm vegetarian options) or return to Kyoto.
- Day 9: Culture and craft day. Nishijin Textile Center (kimono), tea blending workshop, or Fushimi sake district tour (nonalcohol options available). Dinner: Choice (vegan, gluten-free friendly) near Sanjo.
- Day 10: Osaka day trip. Osaka Castle, Nakanoshima museums or Umeda Sky Building; Dotonbori walk. Plenty of veg spots—use HappyCow for latest.
- Day 11: Ohara day trip. Sanzen-in, rural scenery, veggie-friendly shojin ryori at local temple restaurants. Onsen footbaths if available.
- Day 12: Kyoto Imperial Palace Park and Kyoto International Manga Museum. Afternoon shopping in Nishiki Market (verify ingredients at each stall). Dinner: Vegan Ramen TowZen (near Shugakuin; check hours).

- What to seek
  - Shojin ryori (temple cuisine): entirely vegetarian/vegan by tradition. Book ahead.
